title: Universal Basic Income
scope: Unconditional cash for everyone versus targeted transfers or guaranteed jobs.

overview.summary: Should the next safety-net dollar be unconditional cash for all — or targeted transfers, guaranteed jobs, or conditional services?
overview.scope_covered: Universal cash vs. targeted transfers, guaranteed jobs, and direct services: pilot evidence, work effects, fiscal cost, and conditionality.
overview.scope_excluded: Minimum-wage, immigration, and general tax policy; settled historical programs; monetary-theory financing debates.
overview.why_now: Iowa's UpLift pilot just reported its final results, AI-driven job-loss anxiety is pushing income-support redesign back onto the agenda, and states are now split — court challenges and ban laws shutting pilots down in some places even as Cook County and others expand theirs.

stats.label: Full UBI cost · before offsets
stats.note: $1,000/month to every US adult is roughly $12k × ~260M people — $3–4 trillion a year before any tax clawback or program consolidation.
stats.detail: Estimates from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, the UBI Center, and the Penn Wharton Budget Model converge on $3–4 trillion annually, depending on whether the payment covers all adults, all residents, or is capped for working-age adults. None of these gross figures net out taxes clawed back from higher earners or savings from folding in existing programs — how much that recovers is itself contested between positions. This is a structural, population-scaled estimate rather than a fast-moving one; the underlying $3T calculation dates to 2019 but scales predictably with population and prices, and 2025-era estimates (Economic Security Project, Tax Foundation) still land in the same $2.8–3.8T band.
stats.source_label: Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget

stats.label: Current US safety-net spending
stats.note: The federal government spends about $1.2 trillion a year (FY2025) on mandatory means-tested programs and tax credits alone — the base any redesign builds on.
stats.detail: CBO's tally — delivered in a June 2025 letter to House Budget Committee Chairman Jodey Arrington — covers more than 90 mandatory means-tested programs and tax credits, including Medicaid, SNAP, child nutrition, TANF, SSI and refundable credits, excluding discretionary aid like housing vouchers. It's a fraction of a full universal cash floor's cost — the core of the targeted-transfer argument — but it also reflects dozens of separately administered eligibility systems, the core of the universalist critique. CBO's own site blocks automated verification tools, so this is cited via a briefing paper that quotes the letter directly.
stats.source_label: CBO letter to Rep. Arrington (via Cato Institute)

stats.label: Labor-force effect · largest US cash trial
stats.note: The largest, most rigorous unconditional-cash trial in the US to date: $1,000/month for 3 years cut labor-force participation 3.9 points and hours worked ~1.3–1.4/week.
stats.detail: Funded in part by Sam Altman's OpenResearch, the study gave 1,000 low-income participants in Illinois and Texas $1,000/month unconditionally for three years against a $50/month control group. The underlying NBER working paper, first posted July 2024, was revised in September 2025 with larger effect sizes from pooling survey and unemployment-insurance data: labor-force participation fell 3.9 points in the authors' preferred pooled estimate (survey data alone showed a smaller 2.2-point drop), and hours worked fell ~1.4/week, with individual income excluding the transfer down about $1,800/year relative to control. The same research team has since published follow-up NBER papers (on consumption and on parenting/children) from the same sample, with no reversal of the employment finding.
stats.source_label: Vivalt et al., NBER Working Paper 32719

stats.label: Work-hours drop · 1970s US trials
stats.note: The original large-scale US guaranteed-income trials (Seattle/Denver, 1971–82) found work-hour reductions of 9% for husbands, 20% for wives, 25% for single mothers.
stats.detail: The Seattle/Denver Income Maintenance Experiment and its sister trials in New Jersey, Iowa/North Carolina, and Gary, Indiana remain the largest guaranteed-income experiments run in the US before the 2020s pilot wave. Reductions were concentrated in secondary earners and were larger in Denver's tighter labor market than in Seattle's looser one — a reminder that local labor-market conditions shape the size of any measured work response.
stats.source_label: Robins & West (1980), SIME/DIME, via Widerquist/Palgrave Handbook of Basic Income

stats.label: US federal poverty line (2026)
stats.note: $15,960/year for one person, $33,000 for a family of four — the threshold nearly every existing means-tested program uses to define eligibility.
stats.detail: Set annually by HHS and effective January 2026, reflecting a 2.63% price adjustment (calculated on 11 months of 2025 CPI-U data after the October 2025 government shutdown disrupted BLS reporting). 12.9% of Americans lived below the broader Supplemental Poverty Measure in 2024 (Census), which nets in taxes and near-cash transfers like SNAP and the EITC — the same benefits any redesign of income support has to reckon with.

stats.label: Full-time work · Stockton pilot vs control
stats.note: $500/month, no strings, to 125 residents: full-time employment rose 12 points among recipients vs. 5 points in the control group over one year.
stats.detail: The Stockton Economic Empowerment Demonstration was privately funded and unconditional, with no work requirement. It's frequently cited against the OpenResearch and 1970s-trials findings — though at $500/month, a smaller sample, and a single mid-size city, it's a much smaller-scale test than either.

stats.label: Days worked · Finland national trial
stats.note: 2,000 unemployed people got €560/month with no conditions; employment barely moved (+6 days/year) but self-reported wellbeing rose markedly.
stats.detail: Interpretation of the employment result is complicated by Finland's simultaneous rollout of an unrelated activation/sanctions policy for the control group in 2018, which likely pushed some control-group members into work too, narrowing the measured gap. It remains the only national-government-run basic income RCT completed to date.
stats.source_label: Kela / VATT Institute for Economic Research

stats.label: Study scale · GiveDirectly Kenya
stats.note: The world's largest, longest-running UBI trial (started 2016, 12-year arm): overall labor supply hasn't fallen — recipients shifted from wage work to self-employment.
stats.detail: Roughly 23,000 people across ~195 Kenyan villages are enrolled across lump-sum, 2-year, and 12-year payment arms (plus ~100 control villages). Two years in, recipients started more businesses and earned more overall, with work shifting out of agricultural wage labor into self-employment rather than disappearing; lump-sum recipients did best on new business formation. The study runs through 2028 with the next major survey wave expected in 2026, not yet released as of this update. It's the strongest evidence on a long-horizon UBI, but from a very different economy than the US labor market the debate mostly centers on.

stats.label: Child poverty drop · 2021 child-credit expansion
stats.note: A fully refundable, phased-out credit cut the child poverty rate 46% in a single year, the largest one-year drop on record — before it expired.
stats.detail: Child poverty (Supplemental Poverty Measure) fell from 9.7% in 2020 to 5.2% in 2021, driven mainly by the American Rescue Plan's expanded, monthly, fully refundable Child Tax Credit. It reverted to the smaller pre-2021 design in 2022, and child poverty roughly doubled the following year — cited by targeted-transfer economists as evidence a phased, refundable credit can move the poverty rate fast without a universal check.

stats.label: Federal job guarantee cost estimate
stats.note: A national job guarantee at a living wage is estimated to cost $260–354 billion a year net of savings elsewhere — under a tenth of a full UBI's price tag.
stats.detail: The Levy Economics Institute's costing nets out reduced spending on unemployment insurance, Medicaid, and the EITC as guaranteed-job workers earn more. Critics argue the estimate undercounts administrative buildout and wage-competition effects on private employers; proponents argue it's conservative because it excludes the value of the infrastructure and services the jobs would produce. No federal agency has produced an updated costing since; a 2026 House bill (Federal Jobs Guarantee Development Act, reintroduced by Rep. Watson Coleman) proposes only a 15-community pilot rather than a national guarantee.
stats.source_label: Wray et al., Public Service Employment: A Path to Full Employment (Levy Economics Institute, 2018)

stats.label: Earned-income credit's existing scale
stats.note: The EITC, the US's actual working negative-income-tax-style program, already sends $70 billion a year to about 24 million workers and families.
stats.detail: For tax year 2024, the average credit was about $2,894. It phases in with earnings then phases out at higher income, the core benefit-taper design principle — cited by targeted-transfer economists as proof the mechanism already works at national scale, and by critics as evidence its complexity (roughly a fifth of eligible workers don't claim it) is itself a cost of targeting.

stats.label: Benefits lost per extra dollar earned · median
stats.note: Households stacking SNAP + EITC + Child Tax Credit + Medicaid face a median 42% marginal tax rate on each added dollar — and some families hit near-100% cliffs.
stats.detail: About 3 million households receive this exact SNAP + EITC + CTC + Medicaid/CHIP combination — the most common bundle — and face the 42% median rate. Atlanta Fed modeling found a Washington, DC family with one child gets no net financial gain from a wage increase anywhere between $11,000 and $65,000 once benefit phase-outs stack; an Illinois case study found a $1,000 raise costing a family over $25,000 in childcare-subsidy eligibility. Conditionality reformers cite these cliffs as the predictable cost of targeting; universalists cite them as the case for one unconditional payment instead.

stats.label: Work hours AI could automate
stats.note: McKinsey now estimates today's technology could automate ~57% of US work hours — more than double the widely cited 2023 estimate of 25%.
stats.detail: McKinsey Global Institute's November 2025 report ('Agents, robots, and us: Skill partnerships in the age of AI') finds current technologies could in theory automate about 57% of US work hours, versus its own 30% estimate and Goldman Sachs' widely cited 25% figure, both from 2023 — reflecting how fast frontier AI capability has moved. Like those earlier estimates, this is technical-potential exposure, not a forecast of job losses: McKinsey pairs it with modeling showing up to $2.9 trillion of US economic value unlocked by 2030 if organizations redesign workflows around people, agents, and robots together rather than automate individual tasks. How much of that potential becomes actual displacement, and how fast, is exactly what's contested between an AI-dividend UBI and other designs. No newer MGI report has superseded this figure as of mid-2026.

stats.label: Guaranteed-income pilots vs. state bans
stats.note: 30+ US city/county guaranteed-income pilots are tracked since 2019 — even as five states banned local governments from running them in 2023–25.
stats.detail: Guaranteed-income pilots (unconditional, privately or locally funded, typically $500–1,000/month for 12–24 months) spread to dozens of cities after Stockton's SEED program launched in 2019. Arkansas banned local governments from funding them in 2023, followed by South Dakota, Idaho, and Iowa in 2024, and Kansas in 2025 (HB 2101, enacted without the governor’s signature), and Kansas in 2025 (HB 2101, enacted without the governor's signature) — all five pushed by the Foundation for Government Accountability's lobbying arm, the Opportunity Solutions Project. A near-identical Texas bill passed the state Senate in 2025 but failed to clear the House; several other states have considered bans without enacting them. Supporters of the pilots frame the bans as programs being shut down before their own results are in.
stats.source_label: Stanford Basic Income Lab / CGIR Dashboard; Capital & Main

questions.text: Does unconditional cash meaningfully reduce paid work or labor-force participation compared to targeted or conditional alternatives?
questions.why: Most pilots average to a near-zero work effect, but the largest, most-rigorous trials show a real drop, and the flagship trial's own estimate was just revised upward — sharpening what a permanent program would do.
questions.detail: Proponents point to the pattern across geographically and demographically varied pilots (Stockton SEED, the OpenResearch/Altman-backed study, Iowa UpLift, Finland, GiveDirectly Kenya): a February 2026 AEI meta-analysis of 122 US pilots (2017-2025) found the 30 with published, randomized employment outcomes averaged a negligible +0.8-percentage-point change in the share employed. Skeptics counter that the average is misleading: the four largest pilots, holding 55% of all treatment-group participants, averaged a -3.2-percentage-point effect — an elasticity consistent with the broader academic literature. The largest of those, the OpenResearch Unconditional Income Study (ORUS) — $1,000/month for three years to 1,000 low-income adults — had its underlying NBER paper revised (revision dated January 2026): the labor-market-participation drop grew from an initial 2.0 to 3.9 percentage points in the authors’ preferred pooled survey-plus-administrative estimate (survey-only: 2.2), with hours down ~1.3–1.4 per week, with effects larger among younger recipients and the freed-up time going mostly to leisure rather than job search or schooling. Skeptics separately argue pilots are structurally unsuited to answer the question that matters — recipients in a time-limited trial know the money will end, so they behave differently than they would under a permanent universal entitlement. The older negative-income-tax (NIT) experiments from the 1970s ran longer and closer to program scale and found larger work reductions, particularly among second earners in a household, which critics treat as a better analog for a real UBI than a short pilot. There's also a design wrinkle: NIT economists argue their own phase-out structure creates a different, more familiar disincentive than a flat unconditional check, so 'does cash reduce work' isn't fully separable from 'how is the cash withdrawn as income rises.'

questions.text: Is a genuinely livable UBI fiscally affordable at national scale, compared to the cost of achieving the same outcomes via targeted transfers, a job guarantee, or in-kind services?
questions.why: Whether UBI is affordable turns on what 'livable' and 'universal' mean multiplied across everyone, versus paying only people who qualify or show up. Proponents and skeptics are often doing different arithmetic on the same policy.
questions.detail: The affordability case for UBI rests on funding mechanisms that aren't simply new tax dollars matched one-for-one against the check size: administrative savings from retiring means-tested bureaucracies, clawback through the tax system so net cost sits far below the gross 'check times population' figure, and proposed new revenue streams like an AI/data or land dividend that scale with the automation the policy is meant to hedge against. That funding logic has moved from thought experiment toward live policy in 2026: California's May 2026 executive order (N-6-26) directs the state to study 'universal basic capital' — giving people an equity stake in AI-driven corporate gains rather than a cash check — and versions of an AI dividend or equity-sharing scheme have drawn interest from figures as varied as Bernie Sanders, Sam Altman, and the Trump administration, though none has yet produced an actual payout mechanism or cost estimate to weigh against a traditional UBI. The skeptical case is that once 'livable' is defined at a level that actually replaces a living wage, multiplying it by the entire adult population produces a fiscal number that dwarfs any existing transfer program — and that the same money reaching only people below a poverty line (NIT-style) or only people who actually take a guaranteed job delivers a comparable anti-poverty outcome at a fraction of the gross cost, since a job guarantee's cost, while also large, is bounded by enrollment rather than paid to everyone regardless of need. The dispute is less about one disputed figure than about which baseline — gross vs. net cost, per-person vs. per-participant — each side treats as the honest one.

questions.text: Should eligibility for public income support be unconditional and universal, or does legitimacy and sustainability require means-testing or a work/effort test?
questions.why: Universalists treat unconditionality as the point: trust over gatekeeping. Conditionality proponents treat reciprocity as what keeps spending politically sustainable — a clash over what welfare is for.
questions.detail: The case for unconditional eligibility: universal programs avoid the stigma, complexity, and benefit cliffs of means-tested systems — where earning one more dollar can cost more in lost benefits than it gains — and a program that pays everyone tends to build a broader, cross-class political coalition that's harder to cut than one only the poor receive; universalists also frame unconditional trust as respecting recipients' judgment about their own lives rather than requiring proof of worthiness. The case for conditionality: work-requirement reformers argue a program perceived as 'something for nothing' erodes the political legitimacy that sustains public spending over time, that most voters expect safety-net support to carry a reciprocal work or effort test, and that unconditional transfers risk backlash and retrenchment precisely because they break the work-for-support norm that has historically kept welfare programs funded. North Carolina’s HB 859 passed the state House in 2025 and awaits Senate action, with similar bans introduced in Wisconsin and Illinois; Minnesota’s HF 2666 (2023–24 session) proposed a $100M statewide pilot that explicitly walled payments off from other benefit eligibility but stalled without passage — an approach advocates cite against the benefit collisions Iowa’s UpLift later documented.

questions.text: Does unconditional cash outperform in-kind services or guaranteed public jobs at improving recipients' material, health, and employment outcomes?
questions.why: Cash gives recipients flexibility to solve their own problems, but critics say flexibility can't create a childcare slot, a housing unit, or a job that doesn't exist — it can't fix a supply-constrained market.
questions.detail: Cash-pilot evidence reports recipients using funds for necessities, debt paydown, and stability that shows up in improved food security and mental health, and proponents argue that because needs vary person to person, a flexible check reaches more of what actually matters to each recipient than a standardized service ever could. In-kind/services defenders counter that many of the largest costs households face — childcare, housing, healthcare — are constrained by supply, not just affordability, so handing out cash into a market with too few slots or units mostly bids up prices rather than expanding access, an argument that echoes long-standing debates over housing vouchers and similar subsidies. Job-guarantee proponents make a related but distinct case: a paycheck's value isn't just its dollar amount but the structure, social connection, skill-building, and public infrastructure a real job produces, and that unemployment carries costs — isolation, lost routine — that a cash check doesn't address even at an equivalent dollar value. This is a three-way comparison rather than a single cash-vs-alternative fight, and the evidence base is thinner and more indirect than the labor-supply pilot literature.

questions.text: Would a broad, permanent cash transfer be partly captured by higher prices — especially rents in supply-constrained housing markets — rather than reaching recipients as real purchasing power?
questions.why: Pilots pay a few people while prices stay put, so gains land in full. A universal, permanent transfer adds demand against fixed supply — if rents and prices absorb it, the real benefit to recipients could be far smaller.
questions.detail: Pilot evidence is partial-equilibrium by construction: a handful of recipients spend more without moving market prices, so measured gains look like the full transfer. Whether that holds at universal scale turns on incidence. Skeptics point to research showing cash-like transfers are routinely captured by third parties — Rothstein found employers absorb a large share of the EITC, and housing subsidies are partly captured by landlords and developers where supply is inelastic. Since low-income households spend disproportionately on housing, childcare, healthcare, and education — precisely the supply-constrained sectors most prone to price pass-through — the real distributional gain could be materially smaller than the nominal payment, even if headline inflation stays muted. Proponents counter that a tax-financed UBI mostly redistributes existing money rather than printing new demand, that much spending flows to elastically-supplied goods, and that the fix for rent capture is housing supply, not abandoning cash. The disagreement is load-bearing and genuinely unresolved because no permanent, universal program exists to measure these general-equilibrium price effects directly.

questions.text: Do small, time-limited, privately funded pilots tell us anything reliable about how a permanent, universal program would actually behave?
questions.why: Every pilot pays a small group for a year or two, and recipients know it ends. A permanent, universal program would move prices, norms, and lifetime plans — the channels short pilots can't observe.
questions.detail: Almost the entire empirical case for UBI rests on pilots, and their external validity is contested. A February 2026 AEI meta-analysis puts the base at 122 US pilots (2017-2025, $481M paid to 40,000+ recipients); among the 30 randomized trials with published employment outcomes, the average effect is a negligible +0.8 percentage points on the share employed — but the four largest trials (55% of all participants) average -3.2 points, an elasticity the authors call consistent with the broader academic literature. That split undercuts pooling small, often privately funded samples with what a mandatory universal population would look like. More fundamentally, recipients know pilot money is temporary, so they rationally treat it as savings/smoothing rather than a permanent income change — meaning both the reassuring null effects and the modest well-being gains may not transfer. And no pilot can capture general-equilibrium effects on prices, wages, and public finances that only economy-wide adoption produces. The strongest case for relevance is convergence: across many contexts recipients spend on essentials, work does not collapse, and stress and health improve, and newer designs (e.g. GiveDirectly's 12-year Kenya arm versus a 2-year arm) directly test duration. The strongest case against is that the largest, most-scrutinized US trials show a real, non-trivial employment effect once you stop averaging them in with dozens of small ones. Iowa's UpLift pilot released its final results in June 2026 after two years of payments to 110 working families, and it sharpens the skeptical case differently: because the legislature denied UpLift a public-benefits waiver, the cash collided with means-tested programs in ways a permanent, non-exempted program would have to solve structurally rather than sidestep — a pilot-specific carve-out a real program can't rely on. Meanwhile GiveDirectly's Kenya study — the best available long-duration test — shows recipients still spending roughly 12% more than control households up to seven years after enrollment, with a 10-year follow-up forthcoming, though the full 12-year vs. 2-year vs. lump-sum comparison won't complete until 2028.

positions.name: Welfare-State Defender
positions.steelman: Markets for care, housing and health are broken — building supply beats mailing checks.
positions.description: Poverty in childcare, housing, and health care isn't a shortage of dollars in people's pockets — it's a shortage of childcare seats, housing units, and clinic appointments, rationed by geography, licensing, and provider capacity that a check can't conjure into existence. Hand someone cash for a broken market and the price just rises to meet it, or they wait on the same list anyway; build the service and everyone gets it, free at the point of use, for good. Quebec proved the point: its $5-a-day universal childcare didn't hand mothers a stipend, it built the slots, and maternal employment ended up 12 points higher by age 50 with lifetime earnings up 27%, because the barrier was supply, not income. It's also the cheaper path: UCL's costed blueprint puts full expansion of shelter, transport, and information services at roughly 2.3% of GDP versus close to 13% of GDP for comparable-value cash — fix the market, don't just subsidize its dysfunction.
positions.detail: The case descends from the postwar Beveridge/NHS tradition of universal, free-at-point-of-use provision, and was formalized as an explicit rival to cash-first UBI proposals in UCL Institute for Global Prosperity's 2017 prospectus (Portes, Reed & Percy), expanded into Anna Coote and Andrew Percy's "The Case for Universal Basic Services" (2020). Gøsta Esping-Andersen's "social investment" welfare-state research supplies the academic backbone: Nordic states that built out universal childcare and active labor-market services, rather than leaning on cash transfers, post higher female employment and less inheritance of poverty across generations than cash-heavy regimes. There's real internal debate about how far the "basic" list should extend — Coote keeps a residual means-tested cash floor for people below the poverty line rather than proposing services replace all cash outright, arguing services and an income floor are complements, not substitutes. Critics, including sympathetic economists, worry state-run provision means rationing and NHS-style waitlists instead of consumer choice; proponents counter that's a funding and governance failure, not an argument for cash, and point to Quebec's own mixed record as proof of the stakes — the same reform that raised maternal employment also showed worse child behavioral outcomes in its underfunded early rollout, which the movement reads as a case for funding services properly, not abandoning them for a check. In the U.S., care-economy organizers like Ai-jen Poo and the National Domestic Workers Alliance have pushed the same logic into the childcare and eldercare fights of the 2020s, while the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities has long resisted proposals to "cash out" food stamps and housing vouchers, on the grounds that in-kind delivery reaches the intended need — nutrition, shelter — more reliably than an equivalent cash sum would. The case has since moved from blueprint to pilot: UCL's Institute for Global Prosperity is running a live Universal Basic Services trial in Camden, London, delivering free transport, food, and digital-access services rather than cash, explicitly framed as "eating the elephant" one service at a time rather than waiting for a full national rollout. A 2025 study of Quebec's reform reinforced the original case further: cheaper, earlier childcare access didn't just raise maternal employment, it let mothers reallocate toward employers previously closed to new parents, with those firms then posting better performance from the resulting influx of experienced workers — the kind of supply-side, market-restructuring effect the position says cash alone could never produce.
positions.proponents: Anna Coote, Andrew Percy, Jonathan Portes, Gøsta Esping-Andersen, Ai-jen Poo, Robert Greenstein / Center on Budget and Policy Priorities
positions.representative_name: The Case for Universal Basic Services (Coote & Percy, 2020) / UCL Institute for Global Prosperity
positions.representative_note: The movement's clearest costed blueprint — full expansion of shelter, transport and information services priced at roughly 2.3% of GDP versus roughly 13% of GDP for a comparable-value UBI.

positions.name: Work-Requirement Reformer
positions.steelman: Aid should reward work, not replace it — a check with no expectations abandons the poor.
positions.description: Support tied to work is not a punishment; it is respect — money given without expectation strands people outside the labor market and hollows out the dignity that only earned participation provides, while an unconditional entitlement forfeits the political consensus that keeps a safety net funded at all. The 1996 reform proved the point: after work requirements replaced open-ended cash aid, employment among single mothers rose from 57% in 1993 to 73% by 2000, and poverty among single women with children fell from 42% to 34% — a level never before reached. Congress extended the same logic in 2025: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act imposed the first-ever federal work requirement on Medicaid and tightened SNAP's, on the theory that benefits without an expectation to work erode both the recipient's footing and the public's willingness to pay for the program. Conditionality is what makes generosity durable.
positions.detail: Our lineage runs through the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, which abolished Aid to Families with Dependent Children and created Temporary Assistance for Needy Families — time-limited aid contingent on work or preparation for it. Lawrence Mead gave the idea its theoretical spine: a safety net is a reciprocal social contract, not a one-way transfer, and benefits carry obligations because obligations are what reconnect the disconnected poor to mainstream life. We do not pretend the record is spotless — caseloads fell faster than deep poverty, the poorest fifth of single-mother households lost disposable income in the immediate aftermath, and the employment gains stalled after 2000. Our internal debates are real: how generous the wage subsidies and childcare supports must be to make work pay, whether time limits should bend in recessions, how to extend work expectations to non-custodial men. But the core holds against universal basic income and no-strings cash alike. Work-tested support of the kind Oren Cass and American Compass now champion keeps people attached to the labor market, preserves the taxpayer legitimacy that any redistribution depends on, and treats recipients as citizens with something to contribute rather than mouths to be quieted with a monthly deposit. That fight reopened in 2025: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed July 4, 2025) imposed Medicaid's first-ever federal work requirement — 80 hours a month for adults 19-64 without qualifying exemptions — and tightened SNAP's age and exemption rules; CMS issued its implementing rule in mid-2026, a handful of states (Nebraska, Montana) went live ahead of schedule, and the rest face a January 2027 federal deadline. The Foundation for Government Accountability supplied much of the research, polling, and testimony behind the push, citing its own polling that 73% of likely voters back requiring able-bodied adults without young children to work, train, or volunteer to keep Medicaid; the Congressional Budget Office estimates the Medicaid provisions alone will cut federal spending by $326 billion over ten years, while critics at KFF and elsewhere warn millions will lose coverage to paperwork burden rather than actual nonwork. Proponents, including Robert Rector — still active in 2025-26 commentary as the reform's original architect — read that trade as the same one made in 1996: real savings and real behavioral change in exchange for real administrative friction, a filter toward the program's intended recipients rather than a bug to be engineered away.
positions.proponents: Lawrence Mead, Ron Haskins, Robert Rector (Heritage Foundation), Oren Cass (American Compass), Foundation for Government Accountability
positions.representative_note: The principal academic exponent of work requirements; his paternalism-as-social-contract theory supplied the intellectual basis for the 1996 reform.

positions.name: UBI Universalist
positions.steelman: Unconditional cash trusts people over bureaucracy — and work doesn't stop.
positions.description: Every person deserves a floor under them simply for existing — not because they proved need to a caseworker or cleared an eligibility test, but because dignity and freedom shouldn't be rationed by bureaucracy. Cash, unpoliced and unconditional, respects people as the best judges of their own lives, and it doesn't stop them working: Jones and Marinescu's peer-reviewed study of four decades of Alaska's Permanent Fund dividend found no overall drop in employment, and GiveDirectly's Kenya trial (the largest, longest-running basic income experiment in the world) found recipients started more businesses and earned more, not less. A 2025 follow-up to America's own largest cash trial found the identical $1,000-a-month payment improved parenting quality and raised spending on kids, especially in the poorest and single-parent households — proof unconditional cash builds responsibility rather than eroding it. As automation puts a widening share of jobs at risk, a universal dividend funded by taxing capital, land, or the compute and data behind AI is the one mechanism built to reach everyone before the next disruption hits, without first making anyone prove they're deserving.
positions.detail: The unconditional wing traces through Milton Friedman's negative-income-tax debates and Martin Luther King Jr.'s call for a guaranteed income, then sharpened into today's form via Andrew Yang's 2020 "Freedom Dividend" campaign — a proposed $1,000/month to every American adult that put UBI into mainstream U.S. politics and left polls showing roughly two-thirds of Americans favorable to some basic-income concept. Writers and researchers including Scott Santens, Karl Widerquist (co-founder of the U.S. Basic Income Guarantee Network and editor of Basic Income Studies), Guy Standing, and Rutger Bregman argue a dividend must be universal and unconditional specifically to avoid the stigma, administrative error, and clawback penalties — implicit marginal tax rates that can top 80% — that undermine means-tested alternatives. Internally, universalists disagree mainly on funding mechanism: a value-added tax (Yang), a land-value or carbon dividend, or a newer "AI dividend" that treats the compute and data behind automation as a commons to be taxed and redistributed, extending the logic Alaska has run on oil wealth since 1982. Tellingly, universalists don't lean on the widely publicized 2024 OpenResearch trial (funded by Sam Altman) — where a $1,000/month unconditional payment reduced hours worked by roughly 1-2 hours per week (the January 2026 NBER revision roughly doubled the initially reported effect) — as their central evidence; instead they point to Alaska's four-decade natural experiment and GiveDirectly's ongoing Kenya study, both of which found no net work disincentive. They read OpenResearch's result not as a refutation but as people rationally using a temporary, geographically limited pilot to buy time for job search, caregiving, or schooling — exactly the freedom the policy is meant to enable, not evidence against it. The funding debate sharpened through 2026: Sam Altman, whose company funded that same OpenResearch trial, told The Atlantic in April he no longer believes in cash UBI "as much as I once did," and by July was floating OpenAI donating roughly 5% of its equity — about $320 per American household — into a public sovereign wealth fund rather than a recurring check. Bernie Sanders went further, introducing the American AI Sovereign Wealth Fund Act in June 2026 to take 50% equity stakes from major AI firms into a roughly $7 trillion public fund paying dividends over $1,000 a year, while California's governor ordered state agencies to study AI's labor-market impact and equity-based alternatives to layoffs. Universalists read this as their "tax the automation, distribute the dividend" logic winning converts across the political spectrum, even as it forks into rival cash-versus-equity implementations the movement hasn't reconciled — Widerquist and Santens continue to insist the payment must be a recurring, liquid, unconditional cash dividend, not a locked equity stake subject to market swings and vesting rules, to deliver the freedom and stability the position is built on.
positions.proponents: Andrew Yang, Scott Santens, Karl Widerquist, Guy Standing, Rutger Bregman, GiveDirectly, Sen. Bernie Sanders
positions.representative_note: Full-time basic income advocate and writer since 2013, crowdfunded his own $1,000/month unconditional income via Patreon to demonstrate the concept; Rutger Bregman has called him "by far, the most effective basic income activist out there."

positions.name: Targeted-Transfer Economist
positions.steelman: Target the dollar where it's needed — same poverty relief at a fraction of the cost.
positions.description: Every transfer dollar should do the most good it can, and a dollar sent to someone earning $150,000 does far less good than the same dollar sent to someone earning nothing, so support should phase out smoothly as income rises rather than mailing an identical check to every household regardless of need. This isn't a new idea: Milton Friedman proposed exactly this negative income tax in 1962, riding on the tax return that already measures income, with no new bureaucracy required. It already works at scale: the Earned Income Tax Credit channels roughly $70 billion a year to about 24 million workers and families and lifts about 4.4 million people out of poverty (Supplemental Poverty Measure, 2024), and a $1,000 increase in EITC benefits raises employment 7.3 percentage points while cutting after-tax poverty 9.4 points. Compare that to the alternative: a UBI generous enough to matter, say $1,000 a month for every U.S. adult, prices out near $3 trillion a year (nearly the entire federal government's annual revenue) for the same or worse poverty impact once middle- and high-income households are cut in, so targeting is what lets a finite budget actually hit its goal instead of spreading thin on people who don't need it.
positions.detail: The negative income tax traces to Milton and Rose Friedman's 1962 "Capitalism and Freedom," where the pitch was as much about administrative sanity as generosity: replace the sprawling tangle of food stamps, housing subsidies, and categorical welfare offices with one clean, means-tested cash transfer run through the IRS, phased out as earned income rises. Richard Nixon's Family Assistance Plan (1969-72) and several 1970s NIT field experiments (Seattle/Denver, Gary, New Jersey) were direct descendants, and though FAP died in Congress, the phase-out logic survived and was absorbed into the Earned Income Tax Credit, expanded repeatedly since 1975 under both parties precisely because it targets working low-income households rather than spraying cash universally. The strongest contemporary academic case comes from Hilary Hoynes and Jesse Rothstein's NBER work directly costing out UBI against the existing U.S. safety net: they find a UBI generous enough to meaningfully help poor families would be so expensive that even zeroing out every existing means-tested program (food stamps, EITC, housing aid, disability, roughly half of federal social spending) would barely dent the bill, and that a flat universal payment sends disproportionately more money to childless, non-elderly, non-disabled, and middle-income households than the targeted system it would replace. Robert Moffitt's decades of research cataloguing means-tested transfer programs (collected in his NBER-sponsored "Economics of Means-Tested Transfer Programs" volumes) is the field's reference point for how phase-outs, work incentives, and program interactions actually perform in practice. The position's own internal fight is over how steep to make the phase-out: taper too fast and overlapping programs stack into punishing effective marginal tax rates near the poverty line (the "welfare cliff" problem economists on this side spend real energy trying to smooth); taper too slowly and the program balloons toward the cost — and inefficiency — of a universal check. That tension, not any dispute over whether to target at all, is where the school's real debates live.
positions.proponents: Milton Friedman, Hilary Hoynes, Jesse Rothstein, Robert Moffitt, the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)
positions.representative_note: Proposed the negative income tax in Capitalism and Freedom (1962) as a single means-tested cash transfer via the tax code, replacing fragmented welfare; Hilary Hoynes and Jesse Rothstein's research finds a UBI generous enough to matter would cost far more than the safety net it would replace.

positions.name: Job-Guarantee Advocate
positions.steelman: Guarantee the job, not just the check: full employment, dignity, built infrastructure.
positions.description: A job guarantee starts from what people are owed as a matter of economic citizenship: the right to work, not just a subsistence check. Government becomes the employer of last resort, offering anyone who wants one a public job at a living wage with benefits — building childcare, eldercare, green infrastructure, and community capacity that a cash payment can't buy on its own. This isn't theoretical: Levy Institute economist Scott Fullwiler modeled a U.S. program at a net fiscal cost of roughly 0.8-2% of GDP annually, self-financing in large part because it replaces unemployment insurance, food aid, and the social costs of joblessness. Argentina's Plan Jefes put 2 million heads of household to work at its peak (13% of the labor force) and cut indigency by a quarter, proof the model scales in a real economy, not just a spreadsheet.
positions.detail: The intellectual lineage runs through Hyman Minsky's "employer of last resort" and Keynes's insight that idle hands, not idle cash, are the deeper failure of a slack economy; Pavlina Tcherneva at the Levy Economics Institute has spent two decades turning that into an operational design — federally funded, locally administered, jobs tailored to community needs rather than a one-size public payroll. William Darity Jr. and Darrick Hamilton pushed the case into U.S. politics with a 2018 paper for the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities' Full Employment Project (with Mark Paul, modeled by Fullwiler) that put a full national guarantee's cost at $543 billion a year, financed in part by a comparable GDP lift and 4.3 million induced private-sector jobs; in a separate CNN interview, Darity floated a higher, wider-participation estimate of up to $750 billion annually, near $50,000-$60,000 per worker in wages and benefits — a number proponents don't hide from, arguing it should be weighed against what taxpayers already spend cushioning unemployment rather than curing it. That case reached Congress via Cory Booker's and Bernie Sanders' 2018 pilot-program bills, co-sponsored by Gillibrand, Merkley, Warren, and Harris, and Ro Khanna has continued pressing it. Proponents lean on international precedent for proof of concept rather than pure theory: India ran the model for two decades as NREGA, guaranteeing up to 100 days of paid rural work to over 600 million eligible workers and raising household earnings and even nearby private-sector wages by tightening local labor markets — and expanded rather than retreated from it in 2026, replacing NREGA with the Viksit Bharat-G RAM G Act's 125-day guarantee; Argentina's Jefes program, born of the 2001 crisis, is the closest real-world analogue to an emergency federal rollout. The internal debate isn't whether to do it but how: a national uniform wage versus locally negotiated pay, permanent infrastructure versus transitional bridge-to-private-sector jobs, and how tightly to tie job menus to green-transition labor needs — Tcherneva's later work increasingly frames the program as the employment arm of a Green New Deal, and her most recent writing extends the case to argue a job guarantee is the antidote to declining job quality in an AI-disrupted labor market. Proponents' sharpest rebuttal to cash-only advocates is that guaranteed income only replaces what's missing from a paycheck; it does nothing to fix an economy that structurally fails to generate enough decent jobs, and it hands the state's stabilization role to a check that can be eroded by inflation or ignored, while a job guarantee resets the floor on private-sector wages and conditions by giving every worker a real outside option. The push remains live in the 119th Congress: Booker, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, and Rep. Ilhan Omar reintroduced the Federal Jobs Guarantee Development Act in 2025-26 — a three-year Department of Labor pilot testing the guarantee in up to 15 high-unemployment communities — alongside a companion Senate pilot bill, S.3864.
positions.proponents: Pavlina Tcherneva, William Darity Jr., Darrick Hamilton, Mark Paul, Scott Fullwiler, Sen. Cory Booker, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Rep. Ro Khanna, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, Rep. Ilhan Omar, Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, Levy Economics Institute
positions.representative_note: Levy Economics Institute economist; author of "The Case for a Job Guarantee" (2020), the field's core policy text

crux.lead: Does cash barely dent work — or is this really about a floor that comes with no test at all?
crux.lead_highlight: or is this really about a floor that comes with no test at all?
crux.subtitle: The labor-supply question is still contested, not closed; running alongside it are cost, targeting efficiency, and whether support should be unconditional by design.
crux.empirical: Apples-to-apples, national-scale comparisons of outcomes per dollar: do phased targeting (NIT/EITC-style), a federal job guarantee, or direct services deliver the same poverty, health, and employment gains as full UBI once benefit-cliff marginal rates, administrative overhead, and take-up gaps are netted out — and whether AI-driven automation displaces enough work to change that math.
crux.values: Whether income support is owed to everyone as an unconditional floor — dignity and trust over gatekeeping, no stigma, no cliff — or is better directed through need, work, or contribution, so that help concentrates where it is lacking and stays fiscally sustainable and politically legitimate.
